Saturday, October 17, 2026

9 am - 12 pm The Persian Puzzle: Power, Politics, Paranoia, Pain, Paradox Auditorium E, Dartmouth Hitchcock Medical Center One Medical Center Drive, Lebanon, NH 03766

All dates: Oct 17, Oct 24

A special 4-week lecture series!

Join David Bisno for a spirited discussion of the complicated relationships between Iranians, Americans, and the English. What was the path by which American hubris, ineptitude, delusions, and catastrophic miscalculations led to the present situation? What part did oil, Communists, Israelis, shahs, and an Islamic God play in the story? We will unveil not a single error but a pattern of English greed and American inattentiveness, bureaucratic in-fighting, and a string of strategic blunders allowing unnecessary crises to become a historic rupture with worldwide repercussions. 

David Bisno, a retired ophthalmologist with degrees from Harvard, Dartmouth, and the Washington University School of Medicine (St. Louis), has, for the past 33 years, developed and presented courses on a myriad of subjects for ILEAD/Osher and for other institutes for lifelong learning across this country and overseas. He is known for clear, fair, nuanced presentations of provocative, complicated topics, engaging his students with energy and enthusiasm. He looks forward to lively discussion.

Cost: Osher Members $95, Non-Members $105

10:00 am Drum Building Workshop with Jane E King Enfield Shaker Museum

$145 – $310

Drum Building Workshop

Build Your Own 13″ Sacred Deer Medicine Drum

Saturday, October 17, 2026
10:00 AM – 5:00 PM

$295 Appreciation Exchange
A $150 non-refundable deposit is required by September 26, 2026 to reserve your space.

The drum is one of humanity’s oldest and most sacred instruments. Its steady rhythm mirrors the heartbeat of Mother Earth and our own heartbeat, connecting us to the natural world and to ancient traditions that have honored the drum for thousands of years. Used for meditation, ceremony, healing, and celebration, the drum invites us to slow down, listen deeply, and reconnect with ourselves.

Join Master Drumsmith Jane E. King for a meaningful, hands-on workshop where you will create your own 13-inch Sacred Deer Medicine Drum from natural materials. Throughout the day, Jane will guide you through each step of the drum-making process while honoring the spirit of the deer, the gifts of the natural world, and your own personal intentions.

The sacred process of birthing your own personal deer medicine drum is much more than a craft—it is an opportunity for self-discovery, mindfulness, and spiritual connection. As you work with the deer hide, wooden hoop, and the elements of water, air, earth, and fire, you will create an instrument that reflects your own energy, purpose, and healing journey.

Your workshop experience begins with a guided inward journey to connect with the spirit of Deer and receive personal messages and teachings. From there, you will prayerfully prepare and lace your drum, infusing it with intention, gratitude, and your own unique medicine. Whether you are experienced in spiritual practices or completely new to drum making, Jane’s gentle instruction creates a welcoming and supportive environment for everyone.

You will also create a matching drum beater (drumstick), completing a beautiful and functional instrument that you can continue to use for meditation, ceremony, music, healing work, or personal reflection for years to come.

Workshop Includes:

  • A handcrafted 13″ Sacred Deer Medicine Drum
  • A matching handmade drum beater
  • All natural materials and supplies
  • Step-by-step instruction by Master Drumsmith Jane E. King
  • Guided meditation and spiritual journey
  • A full day of creativity, reflection, and community

No previous experience is necessary. All materials and instruction are included.

Whether you feel called to deepen your spiritual practice, honor nature through traditional craftsmanship, or simply experience the joy of creating something meaningful with your own hands, this workshop offers a unique opportunity to craft an instrument that will carry your intentions long after the day is over.

Space is limited, and early registration is encouraged.

Investment: $295 Appreciation Exchange
Deposit: $150 non-refundable deposit due by September 26, 2026.

1:00 pm - 1:30 pm Forgotten Founder Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

This new documentary uncovers the history of Mohegan minister and educator Samson Occom, whose fundraising efforts were instrumental in Dartmouth's founding.

Co-directed by Melissa Tantaquidgeon Zobel, a direct descendant of Occom, and filmmaker Signe Taylor, this new documentary uncovers the largely erased history of Samson Occom, a Mohegan minister, educator and Indigenous intellectual whose fundraising efforts were instrumental in the founding of Dartmouth College. Despite his central role, Occom's contributions—and the promises made to Native communities—were minimized or omitted from the historical record.

Weaving together past and present through an intimate, intergenerational lens, the film features three of Occom's descendants—two as interview participants and one portraying Occom on screen—creating a rare dialogue between history, memory and lived experience. Through Indigenous voices, archival materials and embodied performance, Forgotten Founder explores legacy, accountability and survival.

Discussion follows.

Programmed as part of Indigenous People's Month in collaboration with the Native American Program, the Dartmouth Libraries and the Office of Communications

 

This event is free but registration is required.

 

Get more info and register here.

1:00 pm - 4:30 pm Met Opera in HD: Macbeth (Giuseppe Verdi - New Production) Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

Quinn Kelsey and Lise Davidsen take on the immortal Shakespearean tale of the scheming couple determined to seize power at any cost.

Following past triumphs in many of Verdi's signature baritone roles, Quinn Kelsey is the Scottish king haunted by the ghosts of his murderous ascent to the throne, opposite Lise Davidsen—the world's reigning dramatic soprano—as the power-mad Lady Macbeth, whose ruinous ambition damns them both. Met Music Director Yannick Nézet-Séguin takes the podium for a penetrating production by Louisa Proske, a brilliant young director making waves around the world. Rounding out the all-star cast are tenor Freddie De Tommaso as the heroic Macduff and bass-baritone Ryan Speedo Green as Macbeth's friend-turned-victim Banquo.

7 pm - 9 pm Mountainfilm on Tour 2026 Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

An evening of adventure-packed short films that celebrate the love of the outdoors and inspire audiences to create a better world.

Mountainfilm on Tour is coming to Hanover, bringing a selection of culturally rich, adventure-packed and inspiring documentary films curated from the Mountainfilm festival held every Memorial Day weekend in Telluride, Colorado.

The lineup includes thrilling spectacles as skiers, mountain-bikers, free-climbers, all-terrain skateboarders and more push themselves in pursuit of adventure. These stories highlight Indigenous peoples, people with disabilities, and first-time adventurers, all utilizing the power of film, art and ideas to inspire audiences to create a better world.

Oct 17 – Oct 18, 2026 Oval Box Making Workshop Enfield Shaker Museum

$265 – $285

Shaker Oval Box Making Workshop

Saturday, October 17 and Sunday, October 18, 2026

8:30 am – 4:00 pm

Learn how to make your own nest of Shaker oval boxes in our Shaker Oval Box Making Workshop. Guided by experienced box maker John Cashman, you will make five (5) Shaker Oval Nesting Boxes, from Pennsylvania cherry wood. The class will focus on preparing the wood, cutting swallowtail fingers, bending the sides and rims, and applying a finish. These iconic Shaker oval boxes are made with copper tacks and wooden pegs using the same techniques practiced by the Shaker brothers in their workshops.

No previous woodworking experience necessary. Beginners are welcome!

Students who have completed the basic class are welcome back to build an assortment of larger boxes, trays, and carriers.

All tools and materials supplied. Students can bring their own eye and ear protection and dust masks, but we will have enough on hand for everyone. We will break for an hour each day for lunch. There are a couple of meal options nearby, but they are limited. Consider bringing a bag lunch and water/beverage.

Museum Member – $265/person

Non-Member – $285/person

Materials Fee – $25/per person, paid directly to the instructor

Class size is limited to 12. Advance registration is required.

All proceeds from this workshop go to support the educational mission of Enfield Shaker Museum.

Coming from a distance? Why not plan to stay overnight in the historic Great Stone Dwelling? Check out room availability here.

Check our Events Calendar for other events happening this weekend.

Want to know more about John Cashman?

John Cashman has been making oval boxes for over 15 years. He’s been an avid student of box making, studying both original Shaker-made boxes and modern production methods. He’s made boxes as small as a quarter, and as large as a coffee table. John sells his boxes through the Shaker museum shops at Enfield, NH and Sabbathday Lake, Maine. He’s recently had a nest of 15 boxes exhibited at The Fuller Craft Museum.

Learn about the text of the Declaration of Independence, who the key players were, the Enlightenment influence and if the values espoused in the Declaration are still relevant today. Participants will experience an unbiased look at the Declaration and receive valuable content to understand the influences and ideals of the document. They will be able to critically think about the document and have the knowledge of what it actually says. They will be able to form opinions and speak with conviction about what they learned.

On-street parking available. No pre-registration required

3:30 pm - 5:00 pm “Free Speech in Polarized Times" with Professor David Cole & Mohsen Mahdawi Filene Auditorium, Moore Building

Live streamed and recorded on Dartmouth YouTube Channel

Free speech is under assault.  Progressives question its value when weighed against egalitarian concerns.  The White House has targeted universities, lawyers, and the press, among others, for expressing views the administration disfavors.  And a majority of students report believing it’s justified to shout down speakers they don’t like. Professor Cole, who has been defending First Amendment rights for more than forty years, including landmark cases in the Supreme Court, will reflect on the essential character of free speech in our polarized society.  His current client, Mohsen Mahdawi, a Columbia student facing deportation for his pro-Palestinian speech, will follow with an account of his own defense of First Amendment freedoms.  

David Cole is the Hon. George J. Mitchell Professor in Law and Public Policy at Georgetown University Law Center and former National Legal Director of the ACLU.  He writes regularly for the New York Review of Books and is legal affairs correspondent for The Nation. He is the author or editor of ten books, including No Equal Justice: Race and Class in the American Criminal Justice System, and Engines of Liberty: How Citizen Movements Succeed.    

David has litigated many pathbreaking cases in the Supreme Court, including Texas v. Johnson, which extended First Amendment protection to flag burning; Bostock v. Clayton County, which established that Title VII bans discrimination on the basis of transgender status and sexual orientation; and National Rifle Association v. Vullo, which held that government officials cannot use their regulatory authority to coerce private parties into blacklisting a disfavored political organization.  He has received many awards for his civil liberties work. 

 

 
Ethics Institute, Neukom Institute, Philosophy Department, Rockefeller Center, Wright Center

5:00 pm - 6:15 pm DPU Secretary of Education Debate Cook Auditorium, Murdough Center

Miguel A. Cardona served as the 12th United States Secretary of Education under President Joe Biden. While in office, Secretary Cardona focused on the reopening of schools after the COVID-19 pandemic, accountability in higher education, and the expansion of upward economic mobility via education. His initiatives included growth in reading achievement for lower-performing students and the addition of school counselors and mental health experts in schools across the nation. Prior to his time as U.S. Secretary of Education, Secretary Cardona served as a principal and classroom teacher in Connecticut for almost three decades. Today, Secretary Cardona is the founder of Cardona Solutions, which aims to empower schools and systems to develop comprehensive career pathway programs.

 

Margaret Spellings served as U.S. Secretary of Education from 2005 to 2009. She led implementation of the No Child Left Behind Act, a bipartisan initiative to provide greater accountability for the education of U.S. public school students. She also launched the Commission on the Future of Higher Education, a plan to address challenges of access, affordability, quality, and accountability in American colleges and universities. From 2001 to 2005, Secretary Spellings was a White House domestic policy advisor. In that role, Secretary Spellings oversaw the U.S. President's Emergency Plan for AIDS Relief (PEPFAR), the development of a comprehensive immigration plan to ensure long-term economic stability and to secure U.S. borders. Her other initiatives concerned health and human services, transportation, labor, justice and housing.

Add to Google Calendar
7:00pm African American Soldiers and Sailors of New Hampshire During the American Revolution Pembroke Town Library 313 Pembroke Street Pembroke NH 03275

One of the most interesting aspects of the American Revolution is the role played by African Americans in the fight for independence. Both free African Americans and those that were enslaved were key in manning state militias and Continental Army units, as well as serving on the high seas in the Navy and on privately armed ships. Indeed, their service to the colonies was crucial in a conflict that lasted nearly seven years. Prohibited from serving in military units and largely considered "undesirable elements," how is it that these African-American soldiers came to fight for the cause of liberty, even when their own personal liberty was not guaranteed?

Glenn Knoblock examines the history of African-American soldiers' service during the war, including how and why they enlisted, their interaction with white soldiers, service on the battlefields, how they were perceived by the enemy and the officers under whom they served, and their treatment after the war. 

The Pembroke Town Library is easily accessible, next to Town Hall, with no stairs to climb and plenty of parking. We serve light refreshments after the talk.

12 pm - 1 pm DCC Grand Rounds with Erick Lansigan, MD and Joi Carter, MD DHMC, Auditorium E

Dr. Frederick “Erick” Lansigan graduated from Yale College and earned his MD from SUNY Downstate in Brooklyn, NY. He completed residency at Albert Einstein Montefiore Medical Center in Bronx, NY, and completed his Hematology/Oncology Fellowship at the Yale Cancer Center. He joined Dartmouth Cancer Center (DCC) in 2009 and has been leading clinical trials and education efforts since joining. As the Director for Clinical Trials and Clinical Research in Hematology, Dr. Lansigan has helped ensure access to clinical trials for rural populations. He is also a member of the Lymphoma Committee of the Alliance Cancer Network of Clinical Trials. He has clinical and research expertise in Lymphoid malignancies, including Cutaneous Lymphomas. He co-leads a multidisciplinary clinic in Dermatology and Hematology where he sees and treats patients with overlapping skin and blood issues such as Cutaneous Lymphoma and Mastocytosis.

Joi Carter, MD, is an Associate Professor of Dermatology at Geisel School of Medicine and Vice Chair of Faculty Development and Academic Affairs. She completed her dermatology residency at Dartmouth-Hitchcock Medical Center and her Cutaneous Oncology Fellowship at Brigham and Women's Hospital/Dana Farber Cancer Institute in Boston. Dr. Carter is currently co-director of the multidisciplinary Cutaneous Lymphoma Clinic and founder and director of the High Risk Skin Cancer Clinic at Dartmouth Hitchcock. Through these clinics she performs research, collaborates with other specialists to provide coordinated care and works with patients to create a skin cancer management plan to best fit their needs. She is an active member of the United States Cutaneous Lymphoma Consortium (USCLC) and she established the USCLC patient database registry here at DH for research to improve diagnosis, staging and treatment for cutaneous lymphomas.

2:30 pm - 3:30 pm Space and Plasma Seminar - Dr. Michael Hesse, Naval Postgraduate School (NPS) academic Wilder 202 and Zoom

Abstract: Magnetic reconnection is a fundamental plasma process in space-, laboratory-, and astrophysical plasmas. It powers the, often explosive, release of stored magnetic energy, and it facilitates strong acceleration and transport and of charged particles over huge distances. Magnetic reconnection is the engine behind such diverse phenomena as solar and stellar eruptions, particle acceleration in pulsar winds, and sawtooth crashes in tokamacs. Even though magnetic reconnection has far-ranging effects on very large spatial scales, it is facilitated by processes on very small scales. In collisionless plasmas, these processes must involve intricate collective interactions between charged particles and electromagnetic fields in a so-called diffusion zone, which can be, in the Earth’s magnetosphere, just 10s or 100s of km small, while the overall system may be as large as 100,000km or even larger. In the diffusion region, charged particles become collectively decoupled from the magnetic field, either through complex and chaotic orbits in geometries with steep spatial gradients, or through wave-particle interactions. These collisionless plasmas, where classical collisions between particles are ignorable, are ubiquitous in the solar... For Full Abstract Please Contact samantha.j.marcotte@dartmouth.edu

6:30pm The Capital Crime of Witchcraft: What the Primary Sources Tell Us Howe Library 13 South Street Hanover NH 03755

On first impression, the witchcraft trials of the Colonial era may seem to have been nothing but a free-for-all, fraught with hysterics. Margo Burns explores an array of prosecutions in seventeenth century New England, using facsimiles of primary source manuscripts, from first formal complaints to arrest warrants, indictments of formal charges to death warrants, and the reversals of attainder and rescinding of excommunications years after the fact; demonstrating how methodically and logically the Salem Court worked. This program focuses on the Salem witchcraft trials of 1692 and 1693, when nineteen people were hanged and one crushed to death, but also examines a variety of other cases against women in New Hampshire, Massachusetts, and Connecticut. 

"Margo Burns is an excellent storyteller and historian. Such a pleasure to hear this program and learn about history through Margo's perspective."

-HTG program participant

2 pm - 5 pm Samuel Worcester and the Cherokee Nation 56 Church St, Peacham VT

 Vermont native Worcester was convicted for disobeying the state's law restricting white missionaries from living in Cherokee territory without a state license. On appeal, he was the plaintiff in Worcester v. Georgia (1832), a case that went to the United States Supreme Court. Chief Justice John Marshall and the court ruled the state's law was unconstitutional and etablished that the federal government had an exclusive relationship with the Indian nations and recognized the latter's sovereignty, above state laws.

3:30 pm - 4:15 pm Guided Relaxation with iRest yoga Nidra, and Journaling Rollins Chapel

All dates: Oct 21, Oct 28, Nov 4, Nov 11

The SWC is excited to bring you a mid-week restorative practice* with to-go healthy snacks and journals!

This experiential learning opportunity will take place every Wednesday from 3:30 to 4:15pm. Each session will look something like this: 
- Setup mats and settle into our spaces (5- minutes) 
- Guided yoga nidra (25- minutes)
- Prompted free-write in provided journals (6 minutes)
- Debrief and optional sharing time (6 min) 
- Ending session and putting away mats, journals (3 minutes) 

*mats will be provided

What is Yoga Nidra?

Yoga nidra is a type of meditation practice originating from ancient India, commonly known as "yogic sleep" or "dynamic sleep." It is a contemplative practice that involves following guided prompts while lying in a comfortable position through various stages of relaxation, breathing exercises, and visualization.

This practice aims to induce a state of deep relaxation and meditation, similar to the liminal state between waking and sleeping. This state can provide numerous physical, emotional, and mental benefits, such as reducing stress and anxiety, improving sleep, enhancing creativity, and promoting overall well-being. In this state, you may experience a sense of timelessness, expansiveness, and interconnectedness.

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm Ghattas: A True Story of Murder, War, and America's Undoing in the Middle East Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

A work of true crime and geopolitical intrigue, Ghattas' latest book is the story of what happened when the Iranian revolution collided with the 1982 Israeli invasion of Lebanon and how this led to President Trump's Operation Epic Fury against Iran this year. The tale is intertwined with an investigation into the 1984 murder in Beirut of Middle East Scholar Malcolm Kerr, the father of world-famous basketball player and coach of the Golden State Warriors, Steve Kerr. Professor Tarek el-Ariss, chair of Middle Eastern Studies, will engage in discussion with the author. 

This book launch and discussion is free and open to the public. Registration is required, get tickets here. The event will be livestreamed and recorded.Register here. 

Kim Ghattas is an Emmy-award winning journalist, analyst, and author with more than 20 years of experience covering the Middle East, international affairs, and US foreign policy for the BBC and other print and broadcast media. She is a contributing writer for The Atlantic magazine and a regular contributor to the Financial Times. She was a visiting professor at Dartmouth College for Spring 2026 and a fellow at Columbia University's Institute for Global Politics in 2024. 

Ghattas is the author of The Secretary, a New York Times best-seller about US foreign policy and her travels around the world with Hillary Rodham Clinton. She also wrote Black Wave, a work of narrative non-fiction exploring the impact of the Saudi-Iran rivalry across four decades and seven countries. Black Wave was named a New York Times notable book in 2020 and has since become a reference for universities and diplomats. 

Born and raised in Beirut, Ghattas served on the board of trustees of the American University of Beirut (2017-2023) and was chair of the board of directors for the Arab Reporters for Investigative Journalism network from 2020 to 2023. Ghattas is also a former nonresident senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace (2017–2022), a former public policy fellow at the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars (2017) and a former Civitella Ranieri fellow (2019). 

Ghattas taught with the Middle Eastern Studies program in Spring 2026.

Tarek El-Ariss is the James Wright Professor and Chair of Middle Eastern Studies at Dartmouth College. In 2021, he earned a Guggenheim Fellowship to complete his new book, Water on Fire: A Memoir of War. Trained in philosophy, comparative literature, and visual and cultural studies, he works across disciplines and languages to examine notions of the subject, community, and modernity. His research interests include Arabic literature, culture, and the arts; literary theory, new media, and digital humanities; Nahda and modernity studies; travel writing and the war novel; sci-fi and utopia studies; 18th- and 19th-century French philosophy and literature; and gender and sexuality studies. He is author of Trials of Arab Modernity: Literary Affects and the New Political and Leaks, Hacks, and Scandals: Arab Culture in the Digital Age, and editor of the MLA anthology, The Arab Renaissance: A Bilingual Anthology of the Nahda.

---

The Middle East Initiative is a collaborative effort of the Dickey Center and the Middle Eastern Studies and Jewish Studies Programs at Dartmouth and part of the Dartmouth Dialogues. With generous support from Tal and Ariel Recanati P’21.

5 pm - 6 pm The Door of No Return... | Michael Sawyer Haldeman 246

The Door of No Return: Being-as-Black (2026) develops the foundations of what Sawyer calls Black Event Theory and Being-as-Black through engagements with figures including W.E.B. Du Bois and Toni Morrison and with literature, music, visual art, and other forms of Black aesthetic production. 

 

ABOUT THE SPEAKER

Michael E. Sawyer is Professor of African American Literature and Culture in the Department of English at the University of Pittsburgh, where he serves as Director of Graduate Studies and Director of the Graduate Program in Cultural Studies. He is also a faculty affiliate in Africana Studies. Sawyer is the author of An Africana Philosophy of Temporality: Homo Liminalis, Black Minded: The Political Philosophy of Malcolm X, Sir Lewis, and The Door of No Return: Being-as-Black. His interdisciplinary work moves among Black Studies, philosophy, political theory, literature, aesthetics, and cultural studies, with particular attention to Black being, temporality, revolution, and the world-making capacities of Black cultural production. Sawyer is also an artist in residence at ONX Studios and co-editor of the Journal of French and Francophone Philosophy. He holds a Ph.D. in Africana Studies and an M.A. in Comparative Literature from Brown University, an M.A. from the University of Chicago, and a B.S. from the United States Naval Academy.

6:00pm Benedict Arnold, Patriot (and Traitor) Wolfeboro Public Library 259 South Main Street Wolfeboro New Hampshire 03894

We all think we know the story of Benedict Arnold, the American Revolutionary War general who fought for the Continental Army but then defected to the British. Recalled mainly as a traitor for his 1780 defection, Arnold had risked his life and fortune for American freedom in courageous exploits between 1775 and 1778, when the dream of independence was at its most fragile. As an officer in the Continental Army, Arnold ably led American forces in desperate circumstances against impossible odds, in a blinding snowstorm, through a howling wilderness, and against the extraordinary might of the Royal Navy. George Morrison will take you on a journey through New England, Canada, and New York tracing the complex story of this infamous American icon.

7:00 pm - 8:30 pm Mr. Nobody Against Putin (with director Pavel Talankin in person) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

In this Oscar-winning documentary, a Russian schoolteacher covertly shares revealing footage of the state propaganda machine and its impact on his students.

Pasha Talankin is an unlikely hero—a beloved Russian primary school teacher, known as a mentor and prankster who offers students a safe haven in his office. After Russia invades Ukraine, Pasha's role in the school changes dramatically as he is reluctantly drawn into Putin's propaganda machine. Forced to promote state-sanctioned messages and horrified by the transformation of his school and community, he struggles with guilt and a sense of powerlessness, leading him to become an international whistleblower.

As the school's videographer, Pasha documents intimate and revealing footage of Putin's regime, capturing the rise of militarized children's groups, repressive laws, fervent nationalism and the recruitment of graduating students to fight in the war. When he learns his own life may be at risk, Pasha is forced to plan a dangerous escape from Russia.

Discussion follows with director Pavel Talankin. Programmed in collaboration with the Department of Eastern European, Eurasian and Russian Studies

This event is free but registration is required.

1:15 pm - 2:15 pm Dartmouth Autonomy Seminar Series: Dr. Scott Bortoff academic Spanos Auditorium, Cummings Hall

ABSTRACT: Electric heat pumps are one of the most important technologies for decarbonization,  providing the only viable alternative to fossil-fuel based space heating and cooling systems  in buildings.  Modern electric heat pumps are highly complex, mechatronic systems-of-systems, employing  variable-speed electric motors to drive compressors and fans, electronically actuated on/off  and expansion valves, and highly optimized heat exchangers, all interconnected and operated  to achieve energy-efficient and comfortable performance over a wide range of environmental conditions.

Control of these systems has been evolving for decades, but many challenges remain. Modern heat pumps operate over increasingly wide ranges of temperatures, heat loads, compressor and fan speeds, making robustness of feedback controllers an increasingly critical issue. Manufacturers offer a wide range of products, serving applications from a single room to a large commercial building.  Control architectures must scale to serve this range. The control problem is nonlinear, multivariable, subject to numerous constraints,  hybrid, and hierarchal, demanding careful attention to robustness with respect to model uncertainty.

In this talk, I will tell three stories about heat pump control.  First, I will explain how the  control algorithm currently in production was designed for a room air conditioner, which consists of a single outdoor unit and a single indoor unit.  Next, I will consider a model predictive controller for a  more complex house air conditioner, which has four to eight indoor units.  And finally I will show  an analysis of mass conservation for a dynamic model commonly used to represent thermofluid systems. It has been observed that fluid mass, in this case, the refrigerant mass, is not conserved during the course of a numerical simulation, and seems to "leak."  The analysis reveals the  root cause, and suggests a simple remedy rooted in classical control theory.  I will  close with a brief description of some current research interests at MERL, which include  estimation of unmeasured variables of interest in fluids problems.

 The Dartmouth Autonomy Seminars explore how common principles of autonomy link fields such as robotics, economics, and cognition. It brings together academia and industry to discuss autonomous systems. More information can be found here: https://sites.dartmouth.edu/das/

3 pm - 4 pm PhD Thesis Proposal: Olivia Palmer academic Rm B45, ECSC/ Online

ZOOM LINK

Abstract: Estradiol (E2) and progesterone (P4) are the primary sex hormones that govern reproductive function in premenopausal females. Their concentrations shift by orders of magnitude across the menstrual cycle and pregnancy, and both hormones act on the immune system. Macrophages are immune cells that reside in nearly every tissue, sense local signals, and coordinate the promotion or resolution of inflammation. In the female reproductive tract, macrophages contribute to endometrial breakdown and repair, clearance of dying cells, and immune tolerance during pregnancy. Altered macrophage activity has been observed in hormone-associated conditions such as endometriosis and polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS). Macrophages express receptors for both E2 and P4, but how human macrophages respond to these hormones across physiological concentrations remains poorly defined. This thesis characterizes how E2 and P4 shape human macrophage gene expression, metabolism, and function, and examines how these responses relate to the female reproductive tract.

Multi-omic and functional profiling in an optimized culture system demonstrated that macrophage responses to E2 and P4 depend on activation state, hormone concentration, and exposure time. In inflammatory macrophages, P4 altered cytokine secretion in a concentration-dependent manner, and luteal-phase P4 increased phagocytosis. In anti-inflammatory macrophages, pregnancy-level E2 shifted metabolism toward fatty acid oxidation, and both hormones affected efferocytosis, with the largest reduction at luteal-phase P4. Hormone exposure during monocyte-to-macrophage differentiation revealed a P4-responsive transcriptional program arising before activation, which suggests that hormonal state may shape macrophage fate as well as function. In vivo, hormonal intrauterine device use was associated with a lower proportion of CD163+ cells in cervicovaginal fluid. Single-cell analysis of cervical biopsies from individuals undergoing artificial cycles extends these questions to immune populations in tissue. Together, the findings indicate that E2 and P4 act as context-dependent regulators of human macrophages, with effects determined by activation state, hormone concentration, and developmental stage. The thesis establishes a framework for linking physiological hormone fluctuation to macrophage function and dysfunction in the female reproductive tract.

Thesis Committee: Margie Ackerman (Chair), Britt Goods, and Patricia Pioli

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm "Say you’re sorry!” Apology as Foucauldian Avowal Haldeman Hall 41 (Kreindler Conference Hall)

The Philosophy department presents its Annual Francis W. Gramlich Lecture:

Thursday, October 22, 2026

Miranda Fricker, Julius Silver Professor of Philosophy, New York University

4:30pm
41 Haldeman
Free and open to all

Talk title: “Say you’re sorry!” Apology as Foucauldian Avowal

Description: From childhood we learn what apology is partly through learning that it can be required of us when we do wrong: “Say you’re sorry!”. We thereby learn that apology is something a wronged party generally has the moral right to demand. This complex interpersonal practice of apology plays an essential role in shared moral life, for it is the primary reparative means by which a wrongdoer may take (or be made to take) responsibility for their behavior. At the same time, however, the practice has an importantly problematic flipside: notoriously, making wrongdoers say they’re sorry is a practice that can all too easily deteriorate into morally controlling, coercive, or punishing forms. My aim in this lecture is to offer a model of demanded apology that is capable of simultaneously bringing into view both its positive and its negative functionalities. In order to do this, I invite us to see apology as an instance of the ‘strange’ speech act whose genealogy Foucault traces through many historical contexts: ‘avowal’ (aveu). Seeing apology as a sub-species of Foucauldian avowal, I argue, provides a philosophical model of demanded apology that keeps both its special moral value and its inherently coercive tendency simultaneously in view. 

 

For more information on Philosophy's Annual Gramlich Lecture series, please visit: https://philosophy.dartmouth.edu/news-events/lecture-series/francis-w-gramlich-lectures

5 pm - 6 pm Henry Paulson '68, Secretary of the Treasury (2006-2009) Cook Auditorium, Murdough Center

Henry Paulson '68, who served as U.S. Treasury Secretary from 2006 to 2009 and played a key role navigating the nation's response to the financial crisis of 2008, will participate in a conversation with Professor Emily Blanchard, Professor of International Economics at the Tuck School of Business and Faculty Director of the International Security and Economics Pilot program at the Davidson Institute for Global Security.

Tickets required, sign up here.

---

Henry M. Paulson, Jr., is a business leader, conservationist, statesman, and author. He is the founder and chairman of the Paulson Institute. He also serves as executive chairman of TPG Rise Climate.

Paulson is dedicated to the advancement of free markets, environmental protection, the rule of law, and upholding the basic rights of democracy. Throughout his professional life, he has worked around the globe to support these ideals. His career spans two stints in the public sector, a career in the private sector, and the founding of his own not-for-profit.

Paulson served as the 74th Secretary of the Treasury under President George W. Bush, from July 2006 to January 2009. As Treasury Secretary, Paulson led the nation’s response to the financial crisis of 2008, helping to stabilize the global financial system and avoid a second Great Depression. He also designed the Strategic Economic Dialogue to revitalize the way US-China relations were conducted, achieving major breakthroughs on currency manipulation, trade flows, the environment, food and product safety, and global financial stability.

Prior to that, he had a thirty-two-year career at Goldman Sachs, serving as co-chairman and co-CEO in 1998 and as chairman and CEO beginning in 1999. As a banker, he grew the Goldman Sachs presence in China, believing that it was important to bring best in class practices and standards to China. Earlier in his career, he was a member of the White House Domestic Council as well as a staff assistant at the Pentagon.

Today, he is chairman of the Paulson Institute, dedicated to fostering global relationships that advance economic prosperity, promote sustainable growth, and maintain global order in a rapidly evolving world. A “think and do” tank founded in 2011, the Institute operates at the intersection of economics, financial markets, and environmental protection by promoting market-based solutions to ensure green economic growth. The Institute’s approach is an outgrowth of Paulson’s overarching commitment to engage with purpose and promote global ties in ways that help keep America strong and safe.

In 2021, Paulson helped launch and became executive chairman of TPG Rise Climate, the climate investing platform of the global private equity firm TPG. His leadership of TPG Rise Climate reflects his belief that there is an urgent need to accelerate action against climate change, and that innovative vehicles for private sector financing will be essential for meeting the challenge.

Paulson graduated from Dartmouth College in 1968 and received an M.B.A. from Harvard University in 1970. He and his wife, Wendy, have two children and four grandchildren.

Sponsored by the Davidson Institute for Global Security at Dartmouth.

6 pm - 8 pm End-of-Life Options in the Live Free or Die State Online Lecture

Many people have an advance directive, but few understand how decisions are actually carried out in a medical setting. This lecture examines end-of-life planning in New Hampshire, including the role of advance directives and the critical importance of medical orders such as POLST and DNR. We will cover end-of-life options available in NH now, including voluntarily stopping eating and drinking (VSED). We will also cover Medical Aid in Dying (MAiD), a legal option available to roughly one third of Americans, but not yet here in NH. We'll discuss what MAiD is, what it is not, where things stand in NH, and how individuals are working to bring this option to NH. The emphasis is on practical understanding, clear communication, and preparing for real-world decisions. 

Presenters:
Rebecca Brown is founder and director of the New Hampshire Alliance for End-of-Life Options (www.nhendoflifeoptions.org). The Alliance is a grassroots effort dedicated to better end-of-life experiences for all people and advocating for allowing medical aid in dying in New Hampshire. Rebecca is a journalist and author, founded and directed the North Country's lands conservancy, and is a professional fly-fishing guide. Her commitment to improving end-of-life experiences for all grew from her husband’s death while she was serving in the NH Legislature. She focuses on the policy and personal realities of serious illness, death, and dying.

Dr. Eric Pollak is a family physician and hospice medical director with over 30 years of experience accompanying patients through the challenges of serious illness. He focuses on shared decision-making, blending clinical evidence and judgment with a deep respect for individual values and goals. His work reflects a sustained commitment to making care at the end of life more humane, thoughtful, and aligned with what matters most to patients and families.

7:00 pm - 8:30 pm Maintenance Artist (with director Toby Freilich in person) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

NYC's first Sanitation Department artist-in-residence, Mierle Laderman Ukeles, blends public art with waste management in this documentary on her groundbreaking career.

Mierle Laderman Ukeles, inspired by Marcel Duchamp, pioneered the notion that routine maintenance—from changing diapers to picking up city trash to caring for the earth—could be acts of performance art. 

With never-before-seen archival footage, Maintenance Artist tells a story of essential workers and radical contemporary art. Set during the social and artistic upheavals of the last half century, this provocative, penetrating and funny documentary fills a glaring cultural gap and heralds Ukeles' call for a Maintenance Revolution. 

Discussion follows with director Toby Perl Freilich. Programmed in collaboration with the Hood Museum of Art

1 pm - 3 pm Boo-tiful Lights: A Halloween Lantern Workshop 1 Court Street, Lebanon, NH

Step into the season and craft something spellbinding! Join us for a hands-on workshop where you'll build your very own square paper-and-vellum table lantern with a spooky Halloween twist. Whether you're drawn to eerie silhouettes, glowing jack-o'-lanterns, or elegant gothic patterns, you'll design a one-of-a-kind piece perfect for haunting your porch, windowsill, or mantel this October.

We'll provide all the essentials — paper, vellum, glue, markers, and tea lights — so you can dive right in. Want to make your table lantern truly your own? Feel free to bring embellishments like ribbon, beads, hole punches, or other decorative touches. (If you're planning to add anything on the heavier side, we suggest bringing along a stronger adhesive to make sure it stays put!) You can even bring twine or wire (and clippers) if you want to convert your table lantern to a hanging lantern!

No experience necessary — just bring your imagination and a taste for the macabre. By the end of the workshop, you'll walk away with a finished lantern, ready to flicker and glow all Halloween long.

Caution, sharp tools ahead! This workshop involves X-Acto knives, which are fancier (and pointier) than safety scissors. Please come ready to handle sharp objects like a responsible adult — fingers are hard to glue back on.

2:15 pm - 3:15 pm Physics and Astronomy Colloquium - Dr. Hui Li, Los Alamos National Laboratory academic Wilder 104 and Zoom

All dates: Oct 23, Nov 6

Abstract: What powers the most energetic phenomena in the Universe, from the regulation of galaxy growth to ultra high-energy cosmic rays, and to hundred-TeV IceCube neutrinos? Supermassive black holes (SMBHs) rank among the leading candidates. Yet how can objects so compact exert influence across entire galaxies and beyond?

Observations increasingly point to magnetized jets as the channels through which energy is extracted from the environments of SMBHs and transported into intergalactic space. In this talk, we will discuss the physical processes that govern the propagation, stability, and dissipation of these magnetic energy flows. We will highlight how astronomical observations have constrained our theoretical picture while also revealing important unanswered questions. Large-scale numerical simulations are helping us understand fundamental processes such as plasma instabilities, magnetized turbulence, and particle acceleration. At the same time, laboratory jet experiments provide detailed, in situ measurements that enable direct tests of this physics under controlled conditions. Indeed, plasmas in laboratory jets might even be compressed to fusion conditions so that implications for space propulsion can be explored.

We will conclude with an outlook on how observations, simulations, and laboratory experiments can be brought together to advance multi-messenger astrophysics in the coming years.

Hosted by Associate Professor Yi-Hsin Liu

Zoom Webinar Link: https://dartmouth.zoom.us/j/91888702369?pwd=aUlaVEFYNGZHNlZWL0R3cEVWQXg4UT09

7 pm - 10 pm Kronos Quartet: Three Bones Spaulding Auditorium, Hopkins Center for the Arts

A multimedia concert experience celebrating the power of listening through stories of American cultures that meld, layer and endure. In honor of America's 250th anniversary.

We experience a world of sound thanks to the three smallest bones in our bodies. These tiny bones in our ears—the malleus (hammer), incus (anvil) and stapes (stirrup)—amplify faint vibrations from the outside world, enabling our minds to transform these signals into the aural landscape we know.

Against a projected background, Three Bones combines music, storytelling, vintage recordings, video elements and visual arts to share vivid histories and amplify underrepresented stories. Kronos is joined by an array of luminary special guests to bring three of these American stories to life.

9:00 am Hike into History: Smith Pond with Upper Valley Land Trust Enfield Shaker Museum

Free

Hike Into History

Saturday October 24th at 9:00am

Meet at the Smith Pond Trailhead, off Smith Pond Exit

Want to explore the Shaker trails while learning about the history of the buildings and structures along the way? Then join us for our monthly Hike into History!

Take a hike to Smith Pond with UVLT and ESM! Smith Pond Shaker Forest consists of 995 acres of forest and wetlands in Enfield located between two State Wildlife Management Areas. The three properties combine to provide thousands of acres of significant wildlife habitat. UVLT’s property boasts two waterfalls, numerous articles from Shaker History including spillways, dams, canals, and stone walls, and the beautiful Smith Pond.

In the 1830s, the Shakers dammed several ponds, creating “Shaker Mountain Pond,” and developed a system of canals to deliver water to their community near Lake Mascoma that are still visible today

This hike will be outside and in the woods. Please come prepared with water, snacks, appropriate footwear and layers, and be prepared for sun, rain, bugs, and ticks.

PARKING INFORMATION: Parking can be found at the Smith Pond Trailhead off I89

ACCESSIBILITY: This 4.5 mile out-and-back style hike will have about 931ft of elevation change and has some steeper sections. The trail has divots from washouts, roots, and rocks, and is generally labeled as being of “moderate difficulty.”

All funds go towards furthering the Education Mission of the Enfield Shaker Museum

Here is the link to the google map directions: https://maps.app.goo.gl/Cqd6Qm7VFUNiso4x8

Coming from a distance? Stay at the historic Great Stone Dwelling! Accommodations.

10:30am How the Constitution Helps Us to Disagree Newbury Public Library 933 Route 103 Newbury NH 03255

Deliberation is the practice that holds our democracy together, but does it always lead to better decisions? When citizens only talk to like-minded citizens, the thinking gets stuck and the decisions tend to be more extreme. This presentation gives participants a chance to find new ways to think about a contentious issue using the basic principles of the Constitution: freedom of speech and due process. Instead of carving out one’s (predictable) position in the culture wars, we’ll look at the best arguments on a contentious issue from the view point of progressives, conservatives, and libertarians. By the end of the discussion, participants will have a greater understanding of how the Constitution can help us to foster political friendships.

7:00 pm - 8:45 pm Is God Is (DFS: Myths Revisited) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Aleshea Harris adapts her Obie award-winning play into this explosive, neo-Western revenge thriller infused with myth, starring Sterling K. Brown and Vivica A. Fox.

Twin sisters Racine (Kara Young) and Anaia (Mallori Johnson) are both disfigured from a traumatic fire at a young age that left them in the foster system through childhood and adulthood. Racine is the rambunctious, blunt keeper of timid Anaia, ready to go ham on anyone who talks smack about her sister's disfigured face or her own disfigured arm. They're contacted by their estranged mother (Vivica A. Fox), whom they call GOD, for the first time in over 20 years. They find her ailing on her deathbed, and she reveals the truth: their cold, abusive father (Sterling K. Brown) set her on fire in the bathtub and did the same to them. Her final wish: to make their daddy dead. 

In her directorial debut, Harris brings energy to the landscape, framing the South like a Western frontier in a gorgeous, sweeping blend of urbanism and style, detailing the sisters' love. Though on the road to deliver death, Is God Is pulses with life and through its mythical influences taps into something dark and deeply human.

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited"

Sunday, October 25, 2026

1:00pm Redcoats & Rebels: New Hampshire and the American Revolution Hinsdale Community Center 19 Main Street Hinsdale NH 03451

New Hampshire often gets overlooked in the narrative of the American Revolution, overshadowed by its noisy neighbor to the south. Nowadays, few people know about Paul Revere’s first ride, which was to Portsmouth in December 1774 to warn the patriots that the British were coming to reinforce Fort William and Mary, five months before the Redcoats marched on Concord and Lexington. Nor do they know that two-thirds of the troops at the Battle of Bunker Hill were from New Hampshire. Most people are also unaware that New Hampshire’s Provincial Congress adopted the first state constitution in January 1776, making no mention of royal authority and essentially declaring independence from Great Britain six months before anyone else. And this is just the beginning of New Hampshire’s revolutionary story. This program is presented as part of the New Hampshire Historical Society's celebration of America's 250th.

"Mary was well prepared and is a wonderful educator and speaker. She knows her subject well and her enthusiasm was evident. The slides and stories she chose were perfect for the subject and we could tell she knows a lot more than she could cram into the presentation. Mary is a valuable resource for learning NH history."

- Previous HTG host

The Community Center is handicap accessible; parking is available; and refreshments following program.

12 pm - 1 pm DCC Grand Rounds with Christopher Ott, PhD DHMC, Auditorium E

Dr. Ott is an expert in mechanisms of gene expression and chemical biology. He is an Assistant Professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, and a Principal Investigator in the Krantz Family Center for Cancer Research in the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute. The principal focus of his research is to determine mechanisms of malfunctioning gene regulation and epigenomes in cancer, and to develop therapeutic strategies to modulate gene control factors in tumors. He has a broad background in molecular genetics and epigenetic mechanisms of gene regulation. During graduate school at Northwestern University, he led a team that first resolved the complete gene regulatory structure and enhancer architecture of the CFTR locus, the causal gene of cystic fibrosis. As a
postdoctoral fellow at the Dana-Farber Cancer Center and Harvard Medical School, he led efforts to develop the first generation of bromodomain inhibitors as a potential treatment for lymphoid malignancies including acute leukemia and chronic lymphocytic leukemia. Through these efforts he developed expertise in high resolution epigenomics assays, computational analysis of tumor
epigenomes and gene regulatory networks, and epigenome-targeting therapeutics development. In his independent laboratory at the Massachusetts General Hospital, his team described the complex epigenomic signatures that characterize chronic lymphocytic leukemia and were the first to describe novel chemical degraders of the enhancer acetyltransferases CBP and p300 active in lymphoma and myeloma. His team is currently made up of 6 postdoctoral fellows, 2 technicians, and a lab manager. His team continues to develop epigenomic and chemical methods to modulate gene regulatory targets and deploy large-scale chemical epigenomics screens to identify new cancer drug targets. He lives in Cambridge, Massachusetts with his wife Maya, son Jude (8), and daughter Hero (4).

6:00pm The History of the Kancamagus Highway Plaistow Public Library 85 Main St Plaistow New Hampshire 03865

Considered to be one of the most scenic roads in America, the Kancamagus Highway draws thousands of tourists to New Hampshire annually. The highway, which runs between Conway and Lincoln and through the towns of Albany and Waterville Valley, was fully opened in 1967, but the development of the highway itself took over 120 years to become a reality. Located in the Swift River Valley for much of its length, the Kancamagus is the gateway to the southern White Mountains and is not only renowned for its fall foliage views, but such celebrated natural sites as Sabbaday Falls, Lower Falls, and Rocky Gorge, to name just a few. Join historian and author Glenn Knoblock as he details the development of this Granite State treasure, and offers a glimpse into what the “Kanc” has to offer visitors all year round.

Plaistow Historical Society along with the Plaistow Public Library invites you to another great lecture on the history of NH! Free parking and wheelchair accessible. Any location questions for this event, please contact the library at 603-382-6011.

3 pm - 4 pm PANEL DISCUSSION Baker Library, East Reading Room

Join us for an engaging discussion focused on the exhibit “If I be known dead”: The Story of Ada Blackjack, on view in Dartmouth's Berry and Rauner Libraries. The exhibit explores the Wrangel Island Expedition of 1921-1923 by examining its legacy through Ada Blackjack's experiences as a figure on the margins of colonial ambition.

The discussion will be moderated by Maya Razvi, exhibition curator and the Hood Museum's Board of Advisors Mutual Learning Fellow, Cultural Heritage Technology and Innovation.

Panelists:

Melody B. Burkins
Melody Brown Burkins, PhD, is the Director of the Institute of Arctic Studies, Senior Associate Director in the John Sloan Dickey Center for International Understanding, and Adjunct Professor of Environmental Studies at Dartmouth. In January 2022, she was also named the UArctic Chair in Science Diplomacy and Inclusion at Dartmouth and also serves on the UArctic academic advisory board, Mimir. With over 30 years of experience as a polar scientist working in academia and governance, she is an advocate for policy-engaged scholarship, experiential education, and the support of science policy and diplomacy initiatives advancing sustainability, inclusive governance, and gender equality in the Arctic and around the world.

Jami Powell
Jami Powell (she/her) is the Associate Director for Curatorial Affairs and Curator of Indigenous Art at the Hood Museum of Art at Dartmouth College where she also serves as a senior lecturer in the Native American and Indigenous Studies Department. Powell is a citizen of the Osage Nation and has a PhD in anthropology from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. During her tenure at the Hood Museum, Powell has curated exhibitions including CIPX Dartmouth with Kali Spitzer and Will Wilson, Madayin: Eight Decades of Aboriginal Bark Painting from Yirrkala, and This Land: American Engagement with the Natural World among others. Powell's co-edited volume titled Re-Envisioning American Art: Transforming Museum Practice was published by the University of Washington Press in 2025. She is on the board of directors for the Native American Art Studies Association and has served in advisory roles for numerous museums, arts organizations, and publications. Most recently, Powell curated Cara Romero: Panûpünüwügai (Living Light), the first solo exhibition for Chemehuevi photographer and artist Cara Romero which was accompanied by a catalogue co-published by Radius Books and the Hood Museum of Art. The exhibition is currently on a national tour, opening at MOCA Jacksonville in October 2026.

Liz Shand 
Liz Shand (she/her) is the Digital Collections Librarian within Dartmouth Libraries' Digital Scholarly Engagement Team. She holds a PhD in English Literature, as well as a certificate in Digital Humanities, from the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. There, she also worked as a Project Supervisor for the William Blake Archive. In her current role, Liz liaisons across multiple library departments to shepherd rare books and archival materials through each stage of digitization, including curation, imaging, transcription, and publication. Recent digital collections that she has helped steward include not only the diaries, correspondence, and ephemera documenting the Wrangel Island expedition, but also the premier early-twentieth century magazine on politics and culture in Egypt, Ruz al-Yūsef; and recordings of live jazz performances that reveal the long, but understudied history of Black Creative Music at Dartmouth.

5:30 pm - 6:30 pm Drowning in Tech, Starving for Care - Wicked Problems Series McLaughlin Atrium, Raether Hall, Tuck School

Global healthcare is trapped in two failing extremes.

The U.S. market is paralyzed by technological bloat—an overabundance of capital and point solutions that add administrative noise without actually improving unit economics or clinical outcomes. Conversely, Africa is defined by extreme scarcity, where structural barriers and broken funding models suffocate the AI solutions desperately needed to save lives. This is not a problem with a simple technological fix; it is a structural market failure.

Drawing on more than two decades working alongside Ministries of Health across Africa, Asia, and the Americas, John Sargent D’93, Harvard MD, Founding Partner and Co-CEO of BroadReach Healthcare, will explore how future leaders across business, medicine, and engineering can fundamentally rewire these incentives. Register here.

By rethinking how donors deploy capital, and challenging corporate R&D to view extreme constraints as a strategic asset rather than a philanthropic exercise, we can build a Global Innovation Circle. To John, a pathway to progress is executing a true scarcity arbitrage—catalyzing capital and infrastructure to scale local African health tech ecosystems and bridge the AI divide, while enabling corporations to open emerging markets and port those ultra-lean, constraint-tested models back to the U.S. to fundamentally improve unit economics and cut through the noise of crowded markets.

Join the Centers for Business, Government & Society and Health Care for the F26 Wicked Problems Series Keynote. This program is like a briefing for a CEO: slides break down the problem and fake solutions, the “expert” in residence introduces a cross-sector pathway to progress to tackle the “wicked problems,” ending with a community Q&A.

https://hws.tuck.dartmouth.edu/drowning-in-tech-starving-for-care/

8 am - 9 am MS Thesis Defense: Adrianne Gowie academic Rm 232, Cummings Hall (Jackson Conf Rm)/ Online

ZOOM LINK
Meeting ID: 920 9228 0780
Passcode: 193195

Abstract: Orthopedic implants are widely used to restore skeletal function following injury or disease. However, permanent metallic implants, such as those from titanium, cobalt-chromium, or stainless steel, can lead to complications including stress shielding, ion release, and the need for secondary removal surgeries. As a result, there is growing interest in biodegradable metals that safely degrade after fulfilling their mechanical role. Zinc alloys have emerged as promising candidates due to their moderate corrosion rate, essential biological function, reasonable mechanical properties and favorable biocompatible properties.

Zinc-based alloys are particularly suited for temporary orthopedic applications, such as trauma fixation hardware or pediatric implants, in which removal poses additional surgical risks. Unlike permanent implants designed for long-term load-bearing use i.e. the hip or knee, biodegradable systems aim to support healing over a defined period before safely resorbing. Although unalloyed zinc is biocompatible, it lacks the strength and ductility required for clinical use. To overcome this, zinc has been alloyed with trace elements including silver, calcium, iron, magnesium, manganese, titanium, and copper. In this work, several zinc alloys were synthesized using mechanical alloying of powders followed by their compaction using equal channel angular extrusion. They were characterized using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, Vickers hardness testing, and density measurements. 

In vivo evaluation of the alloys was undertaken using a subcutaneous implantation of 13.25 mm diameter, 1.00 mm thick disks in BALB/c mice over six time points ranging from 1 day to 12 weeks. Three implants were compared, i.e. mechanically-alloyed zinc (97.5 wt% Zn with Ag, Ca, Fe, Mg, Mn), unalloyed zinc, and stainless steel. In addition, a mock surgery control group was utilized. Mice were monitored for weight change and signs of systemic distress, while local tissue responses were assessed via histological analysis using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining.

Thesis Committee: Ian Baker (chair), Jonathan Elliott, and Katherine Hixon

Lecture title: Ethiopian Jews and Blackness in Israel: The Story of the State VS The Story of the People

Abstract: Until today, the historiography of Ethiopian Jewish relations with the State rarely focused on the pre-1975 years. It tended to dwell upon the "revelations" of Ethiopian Jews, their journey on foot to the Sudan, and the high-profile rescue operations that took place in the 80s and 90s. In contrast, this lecture aims to partially fill this gap by viewing the pre-1975 years as a critical moment in understanding the racialized character of how Ethiopian Jews were incorporated into Israel’s polity and citizenship regime more broadly.

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm Reitman and Degrange Lecture - Jason Schnittker Kemeny 105

All dates: Oct 29, Nov 3

Side effects are pervasive but not well understood, even at a biological level.  This talk will discuss the social origins of pharmaceutical side effects, rooted in a multilevel process involving the drug approval process, the uncertain and changing meaning of risk, and patients' fears, expectations, and psychological states.  Many adverse events appear to be nocebo effects, but the nocebo effect is a description and not an explanation.  Nocebo effects are sociological, and should be understood as downstream of social, institutional, and psychological influences.

6:00pm Rethinking the U.S. National Parks Sanbornton Public Library 27 Meetinghouse Road Sanbornton NH 03269

In the famous words of Wallace Stegner, “national parks are the best idea we ever had. Absolutely American, absolutely democratic, they reflect us at our best rather than our worst." But are National Parks truly “democratic”? Who has access to National Parks and what kinds of fantasies do they serve? This interactive program explores the history of U.S. National Parks—as myths, symbols of democratic ideals, and colonial spaces—alongside today’s common National Park activities. Why are visitation rates on the rise? What are we seeking at the National Parks? What do our National Park consumption habits tell us about ourselves? We will look at the rising phenomenon of “selfie deaths,” as well as the broader role of social media in National Park consumption. National Parks may represent freedom for some, but no matter how carefully tended and regulated, they also form part of a planet in crisis. How does climate change fundamentally threaten National Parks, challenging their status as highly valued, protectable spaces? How might we revise the preservation tradition that gave birth to the National Parks to include our own neighborhoods and communities? We will consider these questions in the national context, but also in light of our own state—home to the White Mountain National Forest, which attracts so many eager visitors every year.

The library is wheelchair accessible and has a lift. The library has a parking lot. The program is free and open to the public. Light refreshments will be served.

7 pm - 8 pm AI at 70: Art, Ethics & AI Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

What are the ethical implications of using AI as an artist's tool?

This interactive session will feature the work of three artist-scholars, introducing their work and probing the intersections of humans, machines, data, and ethical concerns.

About AI at 70: What Must Remain Human?

In 1956, the Dartmouth Summer Research Project launched the field of artificial intelligence. It was here in Hanover that the term was coined and the foundational question was asked: can machines solve problems once reserved for human minds? Seventy years later, Dartmouth will convene an anniversary conference to continue the conversation—this time focused not on what AI can do, but on what humans must do in its presence.

The original meeting asked how machines could think. This one asks a different set of questions: Where does AI genuinely improve human decision-making? And where must judgment remain human?

From October 29–31, that inquiry will draw leaders from government, industry and academia, and mark the release of new research on the relationship between AI and human capability. This event is supported in part by The Rockefeller Foundation, which helped fund the original gathering in 1956.

This event is free and unticketed.

7 pm - 9 pm Time Warp Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

A small-town drag theater company stages a shadow cast of the cult classic 'Rocky Horror Picture Show' in this inspiring documentary of self-expression.

Lights up on Rock Springs, Wyoming—a dusty boomtown in one of the country's most conservative states—where 25-year-old Kenny Starling has done something audacious: opened the first drag and queer theater company in town. Their debut show? A shadow cast of The Rocky Horror Picture Show. Kenny's mission: to bring queer visibility, joy and acceptance to the high desert plains of Wyoming. 

Director Allison Berg captures the fledgling Starling Company's diverse troupe of thespians as they mount their inaugural production. From exhausting rehearsals to thrift store costume hunts, the film immerses us in the lives of its vibrant cast, revealing both the exhilaration of performance and the realities of navigating life as queer artists in America. 

Celebrating 50 years of cult fandom, The Rocky Horror Picture Show's spirit of rebellion and self-actualization feels more vital than ever. In a time marked by division and uncertainty, Time Warp celebrates the resilience, artistry and joy of queer communities.

Programmed in collaboration with the Office of Pluralism and Leadership for Queer History Celebration

The Appalachia Energy Immersion Trip is an experiential learning program hosted by Dartmouth's Office of Sustainability. The trip brings students to West Virginia and Washington, D.C. to explore the complex legacies of energy resource extraction and pathways toward a just energy transition. Appalachia has long been a key energy-producing region whose industries — including coal and, more recently, natural gas — have shaped the regional landscape and economy as well as national energy policies. Students will meet with partners working across diverse sectors — energy producers, community organizations, political leaders, and more — to learn about how diverse stakeholders are working toward alternative solutions to help move Appalachia forward.

4:00 pm - 5:30 pm My Neighbor Totoro (DFS: Myths Revisited) Loew Auditorium, Black Family Visual Arts Center

Tender and profound, Miyazaki's animated masterpiece captures the magic of childhood and healing power of nature with a visit from your favorite forest spirit.

In 1958 Japan, Satsuki and Mei move into a charming, old house in the countryside with their father, a university professor, to be closer to their mother recovering from illness in a nearby hospital. The girls, still young and filled with wonder, soon find that the house is inhabited by magical spirits, as is the hollow of a large camphor tree behind their house. As they grow and cope with the absence of their mother, the tree's guardian spirit, gentle and furry Totoro, watches over them and guides them through the challenges of youth.
 
Written during a period of rapid economic growth in Japan, Totoro embodies Miyazaki's concerns about losing touch with nature, the importance of family, and the healing power of reconnecting with both. Through spirits heavily inspired by Japanese Shintoism, he transports us into nature's fantastical world of wonder, personifying its beauty and highlighting the importance of living alongside it.

Part of the Dartmouth Film Society series "Myths Revisited"

12:45 pm - 1:30 pm Lessons From Globalization for the Technological Age Tseng Classroom, Tuck and Online

Globalization was a grand project of new ideas, policies, and global architecture that promised to transform the world for the better. Despite a sweeping vision of efficiency and abundance, the results have been mixed and the political backlash significant. Dean Weinstein will draw lessons from the world’s experience with globalization as we grapple with the opportunities and challenges posed by a new grand project: the rise of artificial general intelligence. As resistance to data centers and other manifestations of technological expansion grows, Dean Weinstein will reflect upon what globalization can teach us about governing in the technological age.  

In person: Tseng classroom, Tuck School of Business. The event will also be livestreamed and recorded. Register here. 

---

Jeremy Weinstein is Dean and Don K. Price Professor of Public Policy at Harvard Kennedy School. He is an award-winning researcher and teacher with expertise on civil wars and political violence; ethnic politics; the political economy of development; democracy and accountability; and migration. He is the author of Inside Rebellion: The Politics of Insurgent Violence, co-author of Coethnicity: Diversity and the Dilemmas of Collective Action, and co-editor of Crime, Insecurity, and Community Policing. For his research, Weinstein received the International Studies Association’s Karl Deutsch Award, given annually to the scholar under 40 who has made the most significant contribution to the study of international relations. In recent years, he has also written on issues at the intersection of technology and democracy, including in a co-authored book System Error: Where Big Tech Went Wrong and How We Can Reboot. 

Weinstein has held senior roles in the U.S. government at the White House and State Department, most recently as Deputy to the U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations during President Obama’s second term. Weinstein holds a BA from Swarthmore College and an MA and PhD in political economy and government from Harvard University. 

Organized by: The Michael G. Fisch 1983 Academic Cluster on Globalization. With support from the International Security and Economics Initiative at the Davidson Institute, Dickey Center for International Understanding; Department of Economics; Department of Government; and Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth.

Evan M. Graboyes, MD, MPH is a head and neck surgical oncologist and health services researcher dedicated to improving the lived experience of people with cancer. At the Medical University of South Carolina, he is a Professor in the Departments of Otolaryngology–Head & Neck Surgery and Public Health Sciences, Medical Director of the Survivorship Program, and Founding Director of Survivorship and Cancer Outcomes Research (SCOR) at the NCI-designated Hollings Cancer Center. Supported by more than $15 million in research funding as PI from NCI, he has led 6 clinical trials evaluating cancer care delivery and supportive care interventions among cancer survivors. He has published more than 160 articles in leading clinical oncology journals including the Journal of Clinical Oncology and JAMA Oncology. His work has helped change the standard of care for delivering timely adjuvant therapy and treating body image distress among head and neck cancer survivors. Nationally, he helps set the agenda for cancer care delivery and survivorship policy through leadership roles at the American Society of Clinical Oncology where he serves as Chair of the Health Policy Committee, the NCI, where he is a member of the Social Determinants of Health Working Group, and at NRG Oncology NCORP, where he is Vice Chair of the Healthcare Access Research Committee.

6:30pm 12,000 Years Ago in the Granite State North Hampton Public Library 239 Atlantic Avenue North Hampton NH 03862

More than 12,000 years ago, small groups of Paleoindians endured frigid winters on the edge of a small river in what would become Keene, New Hampshire. In 2009, an archaeological survey for the new Keene Middle School discovered the remains of their stay and brought to light one of the oldest Native American sites in New England. The remarkably intact site produced evidence of four separate dwellings containing over 200 stone tools and fragments of burned animal bone. These early people, rather than being isolated stone-age nomads, were part of a social network that extended across much of northeastern North America. The discovery and excavation of the site was required by the National Historic Preservation Act, a frequently maligned piece of legislation that in this instance worked to save an irreplaceable piece of the human story.

Free parking, either in front of building or along the side

12:15 pm - 1:45 pm University Seminar: Debt and Credit academic · audience: Alumni, Faculty, Postdoc, Staff Haldeman 246
University Seminar on Debt and Credit will convene twice per term over the coming year. The seminar takes up debt and credit as frameworks that shape economic and institutional life, moral reasoning, and social relations. Debt and credit function as financial instruments, of course, but they also work as metaphors and organizing principles across religion, law, education, medicine, and environmental policy. Our aim is not to arrive at a unified thesis but to build an ongoing forum where colleagues can share work in progress, test ideas, and see how a shared conceptual vocabulary connects otherwise distant fields. We are hoping for a genuinely interdisciplinary group, and no disciplinary vantage point is off the table. A catered lunch by Salubre will be provided.  Please click here to confirm your interest and let us know about any dietary restrictions. If you are not able to make this meeting but would like to remain on the mailing list for information about future meetings, please also use the form to confirm interest.

2:30 pm - 3:30 pm Food, Home, and Words: A zoom conversation with Kim Thúy Dartmouth Hall 105

Kim Thúy is one of the most compelling voices in contemporary Francophone literature. Through her personal and lyrical writing, she explores themes of migration, memory, identity, and the experience of rebuilding one’s life in a new country. Her debut novel, Ru, which draws on her family’s experience as Vietnamese refugees, received the Governor General’s Literary Award for French-language fiction and the Grand Prix littéraire Archambault. She has since published several acclaimed works, including Mãn and Vi, which explore the complex connections between food, memory, displacement, and belonging. Her first play, Ấm, premiered at the Théâtre du Nouveau Monde in fall 2025.

She will be joining the French 18 students for a conversation on food and life.

4:30 pm - 6:00 pm The Law Since Time Immemorial: Creation, Law, and the Rights of Nature TBD

A Conversation with Earth Advocate Chuck Sams

Native American creation stories speak of a time before humans, the creation of humanity, and the responsibilities that come with being part of the natural world. These teachings emphasize a profound ethic of stewardship and reciprocity with flora, fauna, air, water, and land.

Chuck Sams was raised on the Umatilla Indian Reservation in Northeast Oregon. He is a member of the Cayuse and Walla Walla Tribes and a citizen of the Confederated Tribes of the Umatilla Indian Reservation. He also has ancestral blood ties to the Yankton and Cocopah peoples. From an early age, Sams was taught by family members and elders about a Natural World ethic that has shaped his understanding of, and relationship with, the environment.

The conversation will consider how these enduring teachings inform contemporary understandings of stewardship, responsibility, and the rights of nature and what they can teach us about our relationship with the living world today.

This event is part of the Montgomery Fellows Program's Climate Solutions: Wishful Thinking or Hopeful Planning? series.

6:30pm The Ethics of AI Meredith Public Library 91 Main Street Meredith NH 03253

This program explores some of the most urgent moral challenges that Artificial Intelligence presents to society today. Topics include automation and job displacement, deepfakes and misinformation, the role of AI in education, implicit bias, autonomous systems (such as self-driving cars and drones), and the ethical implications of a potential technological singularity. After a brief introduction to applied ethics and the technology behind generative AI, we will examine each issue in turn, highlighting the core moral questions they raise and their significance for shaping sound policies and regulations. The session will conclude with an open discussion, giving attendees a chance to share perspectives and ask questions. Participants will come away with a clearer understanding of the ethical landscape of AI and the tools to think critically about its future impact.

Our building is accessible and there is parking around back off of High Street.
